blocks.text: Among the people of Oman, al-Hasa and Basra, دبا [dbā] is a certain species of locust, small but not edible, as Niebuhr reports, p. 172.

Other names by which the Arabs are accustomed to distinguish the various stages of the locust's life are reported by Norberg in Letter 10 (in fascicle 2 of volume 6 of Björnståhl's Letters), p. 422. 423, German trans., as received from the mouth of a learned Maronite of Aleppo named Germanus Conti. — 1) Beiad [بياض [bayāḍ]], the locust when it has just been hatched from the egg; 2) Sahaf [زحّاف [zaḥḥāf], creeping, see Golius, Lexic. p. 1079], when it begins to creep; 3) Taiah, i.e. leaping, when it cannot yet fly up high but only springs up from the ground; and finally 4) Tajar [طاير [ṭāyir], flying creature], flying, when it fully begins to fly. — The Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic names of the locust have been carefully collected and briefly explained by Tychsen on Ignacio de Asso, p. 47 ff.

"Our entomologists," says Beckmann on this passage, "have not yet examined this scorpion-fighter; yet those who know the way in which the insects belonging to the genera called Sphex and Ichneumon lie in wait for the larvae of other insects will agree with me that what our author has reported about it is not altogether far from the truth."

Dioscorides does not actually say that this is an African name; his words are these: ἡ δε λεγομενη ἀκρις ἀσιρακος, ἡ ὀνος, ἀπτερος ἐτι, καὶ μεγαλυκωλος [hē de legomenē akris asirakos, hē onos, apteros eti, kai megalykōlos]. Nevertheless Bochart's conjecture is not improbable.

In addition there is a very weighty testimony for the marginal reading: nature itself. For locusts have two legs, כרעים, rising above the four feet, with which they leap on the ground. The marginal reading is also defended by Aurivillius in the dissertation On the Variant Reading of the Words לא and לו in the Biblical Codex, §. 4, p. 472 f. of the Dissertations edited by Michaelis. Tychsen, in the Appendix to Ignacio de Asso, p. 56, note, thinks that the textual reading, לא, arose from the fact that the pronoun of the 3rd person singular masculine, לו, was formerly sometimes written with a paragogic א (לא), and that this difference of spelling is noted in the margin.
And in Linnaeus, Syst. Nat., Gryllus Papus, Spinulosus, Onos, Pedestris, T. 1, vol. 4, p. 2068. 2069. 2081, 13th ed.
Compare Michaelis, Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 4, p. 1363.
